keys.statement: If the recycle of unreacted feed grows without bound, the reactor is too small for the feed rate (the snowball effect); this is a steady-state design problem, not a solver one.

plain.title: Recycle of unreacted feed grows without bound: the reactor is too small, the solver is not at fault
plain.when: In a reactor-separator-recycle loop with fixed reactor hold-up, the recycle flow keeps growing (the snowball effect).
plain.do: Check the reactor size against the feed rate before changing solver settings.
plain.why: With fixed reactor hold-up only more recycle can raise conversion, so the loop has no finite steady state.
plain.check: In CHEPTA, reduce the feed or enlarge the reactor and see whether the loop converges. Larsson & Skogestad 2000 discuss this as a control and design problem; reading it as a simulation symptom is Lab's.

decisions.mechanism: With fixed reactor hold-up, only more recycle can raise conversion.
decisions.operation: Check reactor size against feed rate.
decisions.expected_change: A loop with a finite steady state.
limits: Read by Lab as a simulation symptom; the paper discusses it as control and design.

keys.statement: Luyben's recommendation, as reported by the authors: fix one flow in each liquid recycle loop to avoid the snowball effect.

plain.title: Luyben's rule: fix one flow in each liquid recycle loop
plain.when: Recycle flows run away in a plant with liquid recycles.
plain.do: Fix one flow in each liquid recycle loop, as Luyben recommends (reported by Larsson & Skogestad 2000).
plain.why: A fixed flow stops disturbances circulating and avoids the snowball effect.
plain.check: Larsson & Skogestad 2000 themselves dispute this: fixing the recycle flow carries an economic penalty (see their rule on keeping the reactor full).

decisions.mechanism: A fixed flow stops disturbances circulating.
decisions.operation: Fix a flow in each recycle loop.
limits: Disputed by the authors themselves (see the disputed row).

keys.statement: For liquid-phase reactors the authors keep the reactor hold-up at its maximum, which maximises conversion per pass and minimises recycle; fixing the recycle flow instead carries an economic penalty.

plain.title: Liquid reactor in a recycle loop: keep it full rather than fixing the recycle flow
plain.when: You choose what to fix in a liquid-phase reactor-recycle loop.
plain.do: Keep the reactor hold-up at its maximum.
plain.why: Larger hold-up gives more conversion per pass and the smallest recycle; fixing the recycle flow instead costs money.
plain.check: For gas-phase loops Larsson & Skogestad 2000 note that letting the hold-up (pressure) float can be optimal.

decisions.obstacle: Choosing what to fix in a reactor-recycle loop.
decisions.mechanism: Larger hold-up gives more conversion per pass.
limits: For gas-phase loops the authors note letting hold-up (pressure) float can be optimal.

keys.statement: In a gas recycle loop carrying an inert, the purge flow is what sets the inert's concentration (a cited study).

plain.title: Inert in a gas recycle: the purge sets its level
plain.when: An inert builds up in a gas recycle loop.
plain.do: Size or adjust the purge to the inert concentration you want.
plain.why: Only the purge removes the inert.
plain.check: In CHEPTA, scan the purge fraction and record the inert concentration in the loop and the reactant lost with the purge.

decisions.obstacle: Inert builds up in a gas recycle.
decisions.mechanism: Only the purge removes the inert.
decisions.operation: Size or adjust the purge to the inert level wanted.

keys.statement: Design in Douglas's order: batch or continuous, then the input-output structure, the recycle structure, the separation system and finally energy integration.

plain.title: Build a flowsheet in Douglas's order
plain.do: Decide batch or continuous first, then the input-output structure, the recycle structure, the separation system and finally energy integration.
plain.why: Each level fixes what the next one needs.
plain.check: Before simulating, write down the decision taken at each level.
